claims.text: In situ heating in a high-resolution TEM can reveal atomic-scale structural changes in nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Elevated temperatures may produce subtle lattice rearrangements or incipient phase segregation in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are uniform, nearly equiatomic, and in a single solid-solution state at room temperature.
Controlled heating can be performed with an in situ TEM heating holder.
Atomic-resolution images can be recorded under high vacuum while ramping the sample from room temperature to approximately 700–900 °C.
Heating may change lattice distortions and atomic arrangements and may form locally ordered or segregated regions.
Increasing temperature enhances atomic mobility in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Enhanced atomic mobility allows configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy to manifest through lattice relaxation or local clustering.
Lattice relaxation or local clustering can indicate the onset of phase segregation or nanoparticle restructuring.
Heating is predicted to cause observable changes in lattice parameters.
Local ordering or segregation may appear at specific temperature thresholds.
Heating is predicted to alter diffraction patterns relative to the room-temperature baseline.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles have a uniform, single-phase room-temperature structure with consistent lattice parameters and diffraction features.
Behavior observed in the high-vacuum TEM environment may not translate directly to ambient or reactive atmospheres.
Reliable interpretation depends on precise temperature calibration and sufficient imaging resolution.
The onset temperature and magnitude of atomic rearrangements likely depend on nanoparticle size and local composition.
